RagShortTexts: In 374 AD, Picts governed from Highland Brochs & Hillforts, under the paramount rule of Pictish Chieftains.
The polity asserted sovereign legitimacy anchored in Picts dynastic heritage and royal assemblies.
Surrounded by shifting imperial and tribal pressures, the regime enforced loyalty through binding oaths and martial law.

Variants.Content: In 374 AD, the sovereign authority of Picts anchored itself within Highland Brochs & Hillforts, confronting the accelerating tremors of Late Antiquity. Governed by Pictish Chieftains, the state projected imperial legitimacy through dynastic lineage, military patronage, and strict codification of feudal oaths. Emphasizing institutional doctrine rooted in Picts heritage, the crown mobilized loyal retinues and aristocratic councils to repel external encroachment. Beneath ceremonial grandeur lay unceasing vigilance against shifting steppe incursions and frontier uprisings, compelling the leadership to bind provincial magnates to the throne through land redistribution and martial alliance, safeguarding royal continuity amid an era of continent-wide transition.

Warriors sit around the fire in the glen and tell stories of the Pictish chiefs who led them to victory in the hills. When the chief raises his spear, every man must take up his shield and follow the banner into the valley. Their reward is the cattle and the grazing rights that the chief promises to share after the raid.

The chiefs of the glens say they will recognize the high chief's authority only after he confirms their grazing rights in writing. Meet the chiefs at the standing stones and promise them the rights in exchange for their oaths of loyalty. Leave the matter unwritten until the assembly, because a document in the chief's hand could be used to claim the rights for himself.
